title: Amid Heckles and Hurrahs, Anthropic Rings In a New Era
excerpt: Protesters gathered outside the Nasdaq headquarters, in Times Square, as Dario Amodei officially took his company public. Diego Lasarte reports.
content_html:
On Thursday in Times Square, as tourists tried to locate Madame Tussauds and Elmos adjusted their furry headpieces, trading began for the largest I.P.O. in history. Anthropic, an A.I. company that is transparent about its ambition to disrupt the business model of all other companies—and the over-all economy—was greeted with sharp demand for its stock, ANT, sending its valuation to more than $1.7 trillion at market’s close.

Inside Nasdaq’s headquarters that morning, on Forty-second Street, Anthropic’s C.E.O., Dario Amodei, prepared to ring the opening bell. Outside, a small but determined protest was forming. Jose Gonzalez, from a group called New York Communities for Change, had organized the demonstration alongside such progressive outfits as Stop Funding Billionaires and the Democratic Socialists of America. Wearing a brown parka and bluejeans, he handed out protest signs that he’d brought in a blue IKEA bag (“Stop Tech Oligarchy!” “Freeze AI!”).

Ian Lund, a thirty-one-year-old co-founder of the New York Tech Accountability Project, summed up the end-is-near mood: “History could look back at this moment as an incredible failure of the regulatory system to let a company that sincerely believes that its product is going to end humanity go public.”

Gonzalez had a more practical view, explaining that he was concerned about the risk that an A.I. bubble posed to the economy, specifically to the pensions of working-class Americans. “We don’t have any choice but to be focussed on the dollars and cents,” he said. “I think the annihilation moment is so abstract.”

A chant broke out: “Why are you doing an I.P.O.? This A.I. bubble’s about to blow.” A group of French teen-agers paused to observe before heading in the direction of the M&M’s store.

The structure of Anthropic’s I.P.O. is unlike any the market has ever seen, designed to minimize the power of shareholders over the company. The seven co-founders have a lock on 50.1 per cent of voting power, while a separate trust controls the majority of the board. This gives them authority over a technology that Amodei believes has a twenty-five-per-cent chance of causing the future to go “really, really badly.”

At Nasdaq, Amodei posed for pictures with shareholders, and Anthropic staff gave out souvenir pins on cards that read “What we make of this moment, will make this moment.” One attendee described the vibe as “surprisingly hopeful,” adding, “It was one of those moments where they really believed they were going to use this to cure cancer.”

By some calculations, the I.P.O. turned four hundred Anthropic employees into centimillionaires. The combined personal wealth of all employees is now around a quarter trillion dollars.

On the street, the protesters tilted their heads back to see Amodei on Nasdaq’s hundred-and-twenty-foot-tall jumbotron façade. James Inniss, who wore a Black Panthers hoodie and seemed to be the demonstration’s m.c., preached the dangers of unregulated technology as depicted in blockbuster movies. “The Terminator”: “Sarah Connor was in a mental institution because she said A.I. was going to take over the world.” “I Am Legend”: “This is the same Times Square where Will Smith walked down the avenue!”

Nearby, Aber Kawas, a newly elected state senator from Queens and a member of the D.S.A., said that she was troubled by the U.S. military’s use of A.I. in the Iran war. Jes Vesconte, an artist in a leather jacket, was worried about data centers’ effect on the climate.

On the big screen, Amodei could be seen reading from a piece of paper: “I believe sufficiently powerful A.I., working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.”

A young protester, wearing sturdy work pants, said that, compared with kitchen-table issues, the stakes surrounding A.I. seemed higher.“Talking about pension plans and an economic bubble are obviously important,” he said. “But these aren’t really corporations just trying to get money. They’re trying to create a technology so powerful that it can overhaul government systems. This isn’t just, like, a company going public. It is the beginning of tech feudalism.”

Amid the protesters were a handful of investors, so giddy about their impending paydays that they wanted to be there in person. The demonstration didn’t much bother them, although one, a stout fellow in an overcoat, shouted at an activist, “Get a job!”

Dingsheng Li, a thirty-nine-year-old professor of environmental health from Reno, Nevada, stood quietly. He wore a SpaceX-branded hat and jacket, and explained that he’d invested in that company, as well as in Anthropic. He was feeling bullish. “I think it’s going to pop,” he said of ANT. “If this is going to replace me, I’d better own it now.”

Jan-Paul Beukema, a Dutch TV producer who had invested five hundred euros in Anthropic early, thought that the protesters might have a point. “It’s going to be the end of humanity in some way, right?” he said. Once his job was obsolete, he added, he and his friends were planning to open a bar. In the meantime, he was headed to Disney World. ♦
